lines.text: You're about to be fed to six ocean giants.
There's one test your shoulders have to pass: will they fit down the throat?
On the way: a fish dated by nuclear bombs, a whale that has held people in its mouth, a fish that inhales sharks, and one throat nobody has measured.
lines.screen: BOMB-DATED · PEOPLE IN ITS MOUTH · INHALES SHARKS · NEVER MEASURED

lines.text: Teeth don't count.
The rules: just you, nothing in your hands or pockets, no gear.
Across the muscle, your shoulders are about forty-five centimetres: a party-size pizza box.
Smaller adults are closer to forty. Hold on to that.
To pass, a throat must open wider than this red ring, and every giant gets the most generous estimate we could find.
lines.screen: PASS = WIDER THAN THE RING · THE SHOULDER GAUGE

lines.text: Number six: the biggest animal known to have ever lived. The blue whale.
Around thirty metres. That's two and a half school buses, nose to tail.
One lunge can take in more water than the whale itself weighs, and you'd be one small part of it.
So you're floating at the surface. A shadow rises under you, the jaw drops, and you go in with the water.
So what stops you?
The throat.
Most estimates put it somewhere between a grapefruit and a dinner plate.
The widest claim out there is a small beach ball, about thirty-five centimetres. We'll take it.
Your shoulders still win by more than a hand's width.
The whale pushes the water out through its baleen and keeps the krill, and you are a very large, very confusing krill.
Out you go with the seawater. Wet, alive and deeply offended.
And it won't miss you. In feeding season it eats about sixteen tonnes of krill a day, ten cars' worth.
Biggest animal ever, and it tops out at thirty-five. Size isn't your problem.
Number five comes with a strange birth certificate.
For decades nobody could tell how old these fish get.
Then, in 2020, researchers dated the rings in their spines using carbon that Cold War bomb tests left in the sea.
One of them had been alive for about fifty years.
Meet the whale shark. No fish alive is bigger: it grows to about eighteen metres, with a mouth a metre and a half wide, almost your height.
It's night. You're floating under a boat's lights, where the plankton gathers, and the shark rises into the glow, mouth open. Then the glow goes dark.
From inside, the view is a sieve: spongy filter pads in front of the gills, and somewhere behind them, the throat.
Estimates for it run from a quarter to a cereal bowl, fifteen centimetres at the very most.
A cereal bowl against a pizza box. That's not a contest, it's a misunderstanding.
The water leaves through the gills, and you leave the way you came in.
Fifteen centimetres, nowhere near you. It drops in under the blue whale.
Number four looks like the worst idea yet. The basking shark.
The second-biggest fish in the sea cruises for hours with its mouth open a metre wide, wide enough for you to swim into.
It strains about two million litres of water an hour, most of an Olympic pool.
So why don't you end up inside?
It doesn't gulp or suck. It swims with the door open, and the door is a comb of gill rakers.
Drift in and you're not food. You're a speed bump.
Here's how little sits behind that face. In 1977 a Japanese trawler hauled up a rotting carcass off New Zealand: long neck, four flippers. The papers called it a sea monster.
Tissue tests said basking shark. As one rots, the jaws and gills drop away first, leaving something that looks like a dinosaur.
Take away that mouth and there isn't much throat. One old museum account puts it at about ten centimetres, with a sharp bend.
The scariest mouth on the list, and it ends up at the very bottom, below even the whale shark.
Now picture the opening again: just you, and six shadows.
Three have already passed over you. The three still circling are different.
The next one has had people in its mouth. The one after that inhales. And the last one has teeth.
Number three. The humpback.
Run the gauge first. A humpback's throat is normally about the size of your fist.
Stretched for a big meal, the widest figure published is about thirty-eight centimetres.
The widest throat yet, and still most of a hand short. Even a smaller adult, at forty, doesn't go down.
Which is why both people known to have been inside one lived to tell you about it.
A diver hunting lobster off Cape Cod in 2021, and a kayaker in the Strait of Magellan in 2025. Each was back in open water within a minute.
Humpbacks lunge through schools of fish with their mouths wide open, and now and then, you're one of the fish.
Biologists call that engulfed, not swallowed. It's the whale version of biting a sandwich and finding a sock.
Thirty-eight centimetres, the record so far. A lifeguard with a very large mouth.
Number two is smaller than anything yet. The goliath grouper.
Up to about two and a half metres and around three hundred and sixty kilos. A grand piano with fins.
Every giant so far was a strainer. This is the first one that inhales, and you're right in front of it.
It flares its mouth so fast that the water rushes in, and so does whatever is in front of it: lobsters, fish, turtles, sharks.
Off southwest Florida, an angler filmed one take a hooked blacktip shark more than a metre long in a single gulp.
So you're drifting over a wreck. Something the size of a sofa slides out from under the hull.
So how wide does that mouth open?
Nobody knows.
No one has published a gape for a giant one. Scale up a smaller grouper and you get about forty centimetres, and that's a guess.
Forty. Remember the number you were holding on to?
At forty-five, you go in head first until your shoulders hit the corners of the jaw, and everything stops. At forty, on paper, it's too close to call.
Dive boats are full of stories about groupers swallowing people like you. We couldn't find a single one that holds up.
Their real problem is us. They were fished so hard that the United States banned harvesting them in 1990.
Forty, give or take a lot. It edges past the humpback, with an asterisk.
Number one. The one you've been waiting for. The sperm whale.
Up to about sixteen metres and forty tonnes, three school buses' worth.
And unlike everything so far, it hunts things bigger than you. Giant squid.
In 1955, whalers off the Azores found a giant squid inside one, nearly whole, about ten metres long with its tentacles.
Its weight was reported at around a hundred and eighty kilos. More than two of you.
So, what does the ring say?
Nothing.
Nobody has measured it. The closest we have is the anatomist Joy Reidenberg, who says a very big adult bull could swallow a person.
But she means one of eighteen metres or more, bigger than most bulls anyone sees.
And here's the honest part: nobody has ever watched one feed, so even 'it swallows prey whole' is an educated guess.
So you put the ring down. This is the one throat the gauge can't measure.
Could the biggest bulls fit you? Possibly. Has one ever? Two centuries of whaling records hold no reliable case.
Top of the board, with a question mark.
And it wouldn't even be trying. You're not on its menu. You're barely in its way.
That should be the end, and you should be swimming home. But the board still has one empty space, above the line.
So has a sperm whale ever swallowed something heavier than you?
Yes.
In 2019, one stranded on the Isle of Harris in Scotland with about a hundred kilos of rope, netting and bags in its stomach. More than you weigh.
It built up over time, not in one gulp. But all of it went down that throat.
A year earlier, one in Indonesia held a hundred and fifteen plastic cups, twenty-five bags and two flip-flops. About six kilos, a bowling ball's worth.
Remember the rules? You went in with nothing in your hands and nothing in your pockets. No net, no rope, not even flip-flops.
The only gear in this whole video ended up inside the whale.
lines.screen: ALL THE GEAR → INSIDE THE WHALE

lines.text: Nothing in the ocean is swallowing people whole. But it is swallowing what people leave behind, one flip-flop at a time.
So, the final board.

Basking shark, ten centimetres. Whale shark, a cereal bowl. Blue whale, a beach ball at best. Humpback, the record. Grouper, the record with an asterisk. Sperm whale, a question mark. And above the line, our rubbish.
Six giants, one pizza box of shoulders, and you get to swim home.
Which giant should we hold the ring up to next? Tell us in the comments.
Just don't say the blue whale. It's still looking for that very confusing krill.
